surfaces.part: dirt ground with asphalt road patches seen from directly above

answer.evidence: The tile is a flat, full-width 176x192 terrain texture of brown dirt with grey-blue asphalt road segments (crossroads, T-junctions, dead ends) viewed straight from above. There is no front face, eave line, ellipse or roof plane, and the width profile is constant at 176 for every row. As a terrain tile it is a flat top-down surface, so it reads as top_down_slab.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has 5 visible tones per tile, above the grass reference (3) and below the paving reference (7). Near-flat coverage is 2%, so there are no big flat fills. The brown dirt has a fine speckled grain in about 2-3 brown steps. The grey asphalt patches are cobble-like clusters in 2-3 greys. The patches have no real outline, only value separation, and the dark edge pixels carry a tint (0% neutral). The weaknesses are shallow ramps, only 10 distinct colours in total against 5-6 steps per material in Beodeul, and an asphalt look that reads as blue-grey cobble blobs with no visible cracks, crumbled edges or highlights. The dirt noise is uniform and repetitive, with no clumps, pebbles or tufts. It is well above a flat fill but a careful artist would still see it as thinner and less shaded than the references.

The dirt carries about 4 brown steps as a uniform salt-and-pepper noise with no clumps, pebbles or per-area variation. The patch edges have no real outline, only a slightly darker rim, and the 0% neutral dark-edge share confirms nothing is near-black. Flat coverage is low at 2%, so there are no flat fills. Fewer shading steps than the Beodeul 5-6 and weaker material structure make it slightly shallower than the references, so it fails.

surfaces.part: dirt ground with cracked asphalt road patches laid out as crossroads, bends, T-junction, dead ends and a block, seen flat from above

answer.evidence: The image is a full-bleed 176x192 flat terrain tile sheet. Dirt fills the whole canvas (width 176 on every row) and grey-blue asphalt patches are drawn as flat top-down shapes forming a crossroads, an L-bend, a T-junction, dead ends and a square block. There are no front-edge lines, eave shadows, vertical faces or receding side faces, and no ellipses. The column scans show only mottled texture alternation. This fits the terrain kind, so it is a flat top-down surface with no front face.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has only 10 distinct colours in total and 5 visible tones per tile, which is above the grass reference (3) and below the paving reference (7). Near-flat coverage is 2%, so there are no large flat fills. The dirt has a speckled noise texture, but it is a uniform two-to-three-tone dither with little structure: no clumps, pebbles or per-stone shading. The asphalt patches are blue-grey blobs with only about 2-3 steps, a slightly lighter speckle and no cracks, edge highlights or scalloped breakup, so they read as stamped shapes rather than broken asphalt crumbling into dirt. They have no outline, and edges are separated by value alone, which is fine. Overall shading depth is shallow against the 5-6 steps of the Beodeul materials. The road network layout is also fragmented, with disconnected blobs, so it does not read as a coherent crossroads and dead-end network. When in doubt, fail.

surfaces.part: cracked asphalt road patches (crossroads, dead ends)

answer.evidence: This is a flat top-down terrain tile sheet, 176 px wide and 192 rows tall. Brown dirt covers the whole area, with blue-grey asphalt road shapes (crossroads, T-junctions, an L-bend, dead ends, a block and a small patch) drawn as flat patches. No front edge lines, eave shadows, ellipses, or vertical front faces appear in the column scan. The scan shows only noisy texture alternation between dirt and asphalt colours, not a vertical face. The kind is terrain, so a flat ground plane is expected, but the drawing has no front face of 3 or more rows.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a brown dirt field with blue-grey asphalt strips laid in a crossroads and dead-end layout. The measured facts: 5 visible tones per tile against 3 for the grass reference and 7 for the paving reference, near-flat coverage 2%, and 0% neutral dark edge pixels. So on the numbers it is not far behind. By eye, the dirt has only about 3 tones of speckle, and the asphalt patches have about 3 tones of mottling. The asphalt has no cracks, no potholes, no crumbling edge transition, and no dark outline or lighter highlight edge to give it relief. That makes the road read as flat, uniformly noisy patches stamped onto the dirt, which is not a convincing 'cracked broken asphalt crumbling into dirt'. The overall effect is a noise texture, not shaded material. The paving reference has about 5-6 steps with clear highlight edges and per-stone shading. The candidate has fewer steps and weaker structure. It is not flat-filled and not sticker-outlined, but it is shallower than the Beodeul standard.
